notes: To keep the facts distinct, r13 tests the generic-alias target restriction instead of alias identity and receiver type-parameter declarations instead of context-free generic-function values.

cards.statement: Given `func id[T any](x T) T`, a call written as `id(7)` instantiates id with the type argument int.
cards.explanation: The compiler infers the type argument from the ordinary call argument; the integer literal supplies int.

cards.statement: The type `any` satisfies the `comparable` constraint when supplied as a generic type argument.
cards.explanation: Go's constraint satisfaction exception admits ordinary interface types such as any as comparable type arguments.

cards.statement: For `type Count int`, a generic parameter constrained by `~int` accepts Count as its type argument.
cards.explanation: The ~int constraint includes defined types whose underlying type is int, so Count meets this constraint.

cards.statement: An interface type declared as `interface{ ~int | ~string }` is a valid type for an ordinary variable.
cards.explanation: An interface containing type terms serves as a constraint; Go rejects it as an ordinary variable's type.
cards.misconception: Constraint interfaces are ordinary variable types.

cards.statement: A function constrained by `cmp.Ordered` accepts complex128 as its type argument.
cards.explanation: cmp.Ordered includes integer, floating-point and string types. Complex types fall outside its type set.

cards.statement: The compiler accepts `interface{ int | int }` as a type constraint on a generic function.
cards.explanation: Non-interface union terms need disjoint type sets. Repeating int makes this constraint illegal.
cards.misconception: Union constraints accept repeated non-interface terms.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — General interfaces

cards.statement: Since Go 1.24, the declaration `type Identity[T any] = T` is a valid generic type alias.
cards.explanation: A generic alias rejects its own type parameter as its entire right-hand side.
cards.misconception: A generic alias accepts its own type parameter as its target type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Alias declarations

cards.statement: Since Go 1.26, `type Merger[T Merger[T]] interface{ Merge(T) T }` is a valid generic type declaration.
cards.explanation: A generic type's parameter constraint can refer to that generic type, as Merger[T] does in this declaration.

source.title: Go 1.26 Release Notes — Changes to the language

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, `func (s Set[T]) Map[U any](f func(T) U) []U` is a valid signature for `type Set[T any] []T`.
cards.explanation: Map declares its own U in addition to the receiver's T. Its result slice uses U while its function argument accepts T.

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, a generic method implements an interface method when an instantiation matches the required signature.
cards.explanation: Interface implementation depends on the type's declared methods. Instantiating a generic method does not make it implement an interface method.
cards.misconception: A matching instantiation of a generic method satisfies an interface method.

cards.statement: For `type Box[T any] struct{ V T }`, a method receiver `b Box[U]` uses an existing type named U.
cards.explanation: The receiver Box[U] declares a method-local type parameter U, with the constraint inherited from Box's corresponding parameter.
cards.misconception: Receiver type arguments refer to existing types.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method declarations

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, given `func id[T any](x T) T`, the literal `[]func(int) int{id}` infers T as int.
cards.explanation: The composite literal supplies the expected func(int) int element type. Go uses that context to instantiate the generic function.

cards.statement: The package-level declaration `var Étage int` exports Étage to importing packages.
cards.explanation: É is a Unicode uppercase letter, so the package-level name Étage is exported.

source.title: Go FAQ — What's up with Unicode identifiers?

cards.statement: A package-level identifier named cache has scope limited to the source file that declares it.
cards.explanation: Package-level cache is visible in other source files of the same package.
cards.misconception: Lower-case package-level names have file scope.

source.title: Go FAQ — How do I create a multifile package?

cards.statement: Package `example.com/m/b` successfully imports `example.com/m/a/internal/x` within module `example.com/m`.
cards.explanation: An import of example.com/m/a/internal/x needs an importing path within example.com/m/a. Sharing the outer module is insufficient.
cards.misconception: Sharing a module grants access to its internal packages regardless of the directory above internal.

cards.statement: The compiler accepts an import cycle where package a imports b and package b imports a.
cards.explanation: Go rejects a package importing itself through another package; the resulting import cycle is illegal.
cards.misconception: Packages can import one another in a cycle.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Import declarations

cards.statement: A blank import schedules the imported package's initialization as a dependency.
cards.explanation: A blank import triggers initialization side effects even when code uses none of that package's exported names.

source.title: Effective Go — Import for side effect

cards.statement: The go command records hashes of dependency content in go.sum for later integrity checks.
cards.explanation: go.sum stores hashes for dependency module files and module archives. The go command checks downloaded content against these recorded hashes.

cards.statement: At package level, `var a = b; var b = 7` initializes b before a despite their declaration order.
cards.explanation: The initializer for package-level a reads b, so Go initializes b first despite its later declaration.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Package initialization

cards.statement: The compiler rejects two `func init() {}` declarations placed in one source file.
cards.explanation: Go permits multiple init functions in one source file; each serves as a separate initialization function.
cards.misconception: A source file's init function name follows the ordinary uniqueness rule for function declarations.

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, Go initializes the lexically earliest import path among packages ready for initialization.
cards.explanation: Among packages whose imports are already initialized, Go chooses the earliest import path in sorted order.

source.title: Go 1.21 Release Notes — Changes to the language

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, the go directive sets an advisory minimum toolchain version for the module.
cards.explanation: The go directive declares a mandatory minimum Go version. A toolchain older than that requirement refuses to use the module.
cards.misconception: The go directive remains an advisory minimum version.

cards.statement: Since Go 1.26, `go mod init` with a Go 1.27 toolchain writes `go 1.26.0` into a new go.mod.
cards.explanation: For a released Go 1.N.X toolchain, go mod init writes go 1.(N-1).0. With Go 1.27, that produces go 1.26.0.

cards.statement: A module published at v2.0.0 uses `example.com/m` as its module path.
cards.explanation: For a module released at v2.0.0, the path is example.com/m/v2. Its package import paths use that suffixed module path as their prefix.
cards.misconception: Major version 2 modules keep the unsuffixed module path.

source.title: Go Modules Reference — Major version suffixes
